consensus_summary: Mainstream consensus reads 'shadow of death' (tsalmaveth) as the deepest darkness and gloom of mortal peril or death's near presence, through which God accompanies the believer (Psalm 23:4), extended in the prophetic/NT strand (Isa 9:2; Matt 4:16; Luke 1:79) to the spiritual darkness and hopelessness of humanity apart from God, dispelled by Christ's light. Recognized variants include a philological 'deep darkness' reading, Sheol/realm of the dead, the deathbed experience, national oppression, and despair.
book_summary: The book defines the shadow of death typologically as the symbolic 'Way' and pattern of the world shaped like Death's substance — sin, darkness, and bondage whose wages end at the pit or grave (Rom 6:23) — set explicitly opposite the 'shadow of Christ' (the appointed times, assemblies, and humbled Way shaped like His substance, per Phil 2:5-9) which leads through death to eternal life.
consensus_core_identification: Extreme darkness/mortal peril and, in the Christ-light strand, the spiritual darkness of the human condition apart from God — a state or condition one may pass through under divine protection or from which one is delivered.
book_core_identification: A structured 'Way' or pattern of life belonging to the world — sin, darkness, and bondage — that is death's shadow in a shadow/substance typology, terminating in the grave, and paired antithetically with the shadow of Christ.
boundary_disagreement: The book converts a broad condition/experience (mortal peril, deep gloom, spiritual darkness) into a specific typological category: a walked 'Way' patterned after Death's substance, opposed to a corresponding shadow of Christ. This reclassifies Psalm 23:4's valley from mortal danger or the experience of dying into traversal of the world's sin-and-bondage pattern, and effectively excludes or demotes the purely philological 'deep darkness' reading, the Sheol-locative reading, and the deathbed/pastoral readings that the consensus admits. It elevates and systematizes the consensus's 'spiritual darkness of sin' alternative (Isa 9:2; Luke 1:79) into the central identification, adding the sin→wages→grave causal chain (Rom 6:23) and the antithetical pairing with a 'shadow of Christ' that no consensus response mentions.
rationale: The book's central referent remains recognizably within the consensus family: darkness, sin, and bondage associated with death, relieved by Christ's light (Isa 9:2; Luke 1:79 are cited by both). It does not replace the referent with something incompatible; rather it takes the consensus's 'spiritual darkness/condition of sin' strand (listed as common in all four responses) and materially reshapes it into a formal shadow/substance typology with a defined opposite, adding conditions (a 'Way' shaped like Death's substance, wages ending at the grave) and reclassifying key cases (Psalm 23:4 as walking the world's death-patterned Way rather than facing mortal peril). This is real boundary disagreement without core contradiction, fitting REFINED. The antithetical 'shadow of Christ' pairing is a structural novelty, but it modifies rather than displaces the identification of the term itself.
strongest_objection: One could argue DIVERGENT: the consensus core is a condition or peril one passes through under God's protection, whereas the book makes it a rival 'Way' of the world within an idiosyncratic shadow/substance system opposed to a 'shadow of Christ' — a systemic reinterpretation absent from any listed alternative, arguably replacing the experiential referent with a typological one. Alternatively, one could argue MATCH, since the spiritual-darkness-of-sin reading dispelled by Christ is already a common consensus alternative and the book merely rewords it. The cited verses support sin-death linkage (Rom 6:23) and bondage (Ps 107:10,14) but do not themselves establish the 'shadow shaped like substance' typology or the Way/anti-Way pairing, so support is only partial.
